Daily Dose of Data Science en Instagram: "Google dropped a banger paper 🧠

If you write or curate skills for your agents, this one is for you.

Agent skills are folders holding the instructions an agent follows for a task. People increasingly let agents write those instructions themselves.

The loop is simple: run the agent on some tasks, read the runs that failed, rewrite the instructions, and keep the rewrite only if the score goes up on a held-out validation set.

Here is where it breaks.

Working out why the agent failed means reading full traces and comparing failed runs against successful ones. But that diagnosis never gets written down. The only thing saved is the new instruction text it produced.

So when that instruction reverts, the finding behind it goes too. The next round reads the same failures, reaches the same conclusion, and often proposes the fix that already lost, with no memory that it was ever tried.

WikiSkill fixes this by splitting the one folder into three:

1️⃣ Raw traces, written once and never touched

2️⃣ A wiki of accumulated knowledge holding what keeps breaking, what has worked, and every edit tried so far with the reason it passed or failed. Nothing here is ever deleted.

3️⃣ The skills themselves, reverted whenever an edit makes things worse

The instructions can roll back, but the understanding behind them never does.

An early skill gets rejected for being too vague. Instead of vanishing, that rejection is logged. The next round sees the vague version failed and writes a concrete rule instead. Same failure, same analysis, but the second attempt starts from knowing what already did not work.

Turning the knowledge layer off drops the average score by about a quarter.

Two other results worth noting: smaller models with evolved skills beat much larger models running without any, and skills evolved by one model transfer across families.

Paper in the comments!

👉 Over to you: Are you currently logging why skill edits failed, or just whether they did?

#agents #skills #google"

codewithbrij/Dd5a_mmuZwY.caption:
Brij Kishore Pandey en Instagram: "One diagram to understand how an AI agent works.

Follow one request through the animation: "Summarize Q3 churn, email the team."

The agent goes around the plan, act, observe loop three times:
Lap 1 queries SQL for the churn numbers
Lap 2 runs Python to build the chart
Lap 3 sends the email after a person approves it

What the dot colors mean:
Orange is the task and every command
Blue is results coming back from a tool
Pink is short term memory
Yellow is long term memory
Lime is trace events

The parts:
Instructions set the goal and the limits
The LLM picks the next step
Memory carries context between steps
Guardrails check every tool call before it runs
Tools act on real systems
Traces record each step so the run can be reviewed

The email waits for a person because it reaches other people and cannot be unsent. Reading data and drafting a chart run on their own.

Which part of this loop do you think takes the most work to get right in production?

#AIAgents #AgenticAI #LLM"

hackproduct/Dd3stOat159.caption:
HackProduct en Instagram: "Your RAG system probably isn’t failing at retrieval. It’s failing at chunking. ✂️

Most RAG debugging starts with swapping the embedding model. The better question is what your chunks look like. If the answer got split across two chunks, no model and no vector database can put it back together.

Here are 6 chunking strategies for RAG in one loop 👇

1️⃣ Fixed-size: cut every N tokens, with 10–20% overlap so ideas at the edges aren’t cut in half.
→ Good for: a fast baseline, uniform text

2️⃣ Semantic: embed each sentence and cut where the meaning shifts.
→ Good for: long documents that cover several topics

3️⃣ Recursive: split by paragraph, then by sentence, until every piece fits the limit.
→ Good for: most production pipelines (LangChain’s default splitter works this way)

4️⃣ Hierarchical: document → section → chunk, and each chunk keeps its parent headings.
→ Good for: manuals, policies, docs with a clear structure

5️⃣ Modality-specific: text, images and tables each get their own chunker.
→ Good for: PDFs full of tables and charts

6️⃣ Agentic: an LLM reads the document and decides where to split.
→ Good for: messy, high-value content, if you can afford an LLM call per document

👀 What people miss: a chunk that’s too small loses context, and one that’s too big buries the answer in noise. Tables are where most pipelines break. A table split across two chunks means both halves are useless.

Chunk for how people will search, not for how the file is formatted.

📸 Screenshot this before your next RAG design review.
